facts.F1: The plaintiff brought the claim against the defendant on the basis that in late 1999, the defendant deceived him into paying RMB3 million odd by misrepresenting that he was the business partner of the plaintiff's late father in relation to a concrete sub-contract for a construction project in Beijing.
facts.F2: The sum paid by the plaintiff was the defendant's alleged share of the profits made out of the Beijing Project.
facts.F3: The plaintiff subsequently found out that the defendant was not a business partner of his late father and thus the defendant's representation was made fraudulently.
facts.F4: The defendant filed a defence in October 2005, stating that he was a business partner of the plaintiff's late father for the Beijing Project and that he had not made the said representation.
facts.F5: The plaintiff took out an application for summary judgment against the defendant in September 2006.
facts.F6: The defendant, along with three other individuals, filed an affirmation to oppose the summary judgment application in November 2006.
facts.F7: The affirmations confirmed that the defendant was a business partner of the plaintiff's late father in the Beijing Project.
facts.F8: The plaintiff and his sister then filed their affirmations in reply under the summary judgment application on 17 January 2007.
facts.F9: Thereafter, the plaintiff has never applied to fix a hearing date for the summary judgment application and has not taken any steps in the proceedings.
facts.F10: The defendant took out the present application to strike out the action some 32 months after the last step taken in the proceedings.
facts.F11: The plaintiff and his solicitor filed explanations for the inaction, stating that the plaintiff was focusing on his work abroad and the solicitor had overlooked the case due to the setting up of his new firm and debates with former partners.
facts.F12: The explanations for the inaction were deemed unacceptable by the court.
facts.F13: The court found gross procrastination on the part of the plaintiff and his solicitor.
facts.F14: The court considered all the circumstances and evidence before it in determining whether the proceedings should be struck out.

requested_remedy: Claims made by Seacliff include pre-action Norwich Pharmacal orders for discovery against two merchants and two banks. parties: Defendant: Decca Limited, Tai Ping Carpets Limited, The Hongkong and Shanghai Banking Corporation Limited, Credit Lyonnais, Benwick International Limited

facts.F1: Seacliff, as manager of the Shanghai Centre, approved a redevelopment and refurbishment programme and a budget of US$49m, to be undertaken between 1995 and 2000.
facts.F2: In June 1995 Benswick was engaged to provide project management services and services for the supply of, inter alia, carpet, furnishings and lighting, for a monthly fee.
facts.F3: Four companies incorporated in Guangzhou (the Guangzhou companies) came to be engaged in the project, for reasons not apparent to the investigator Duperouzel.
facts.F4: The project was completed by December 2000 at a total cost, revealed by the investigation, of US$84m., US$35m. over the budget of US$49m.
facts.F5: According to a report completed by surveyors engaged by Kroll, the value of the work actually undertaken was closer to US$41m., representing an overspend of US$43m.
facts.F6: About US$42m. was paid to or through the Guangzhou companies.
facts.F7: There were accounting irregularities, such as Benswick claiming reimbursement from Seacliff for the sum of $16,831,568 purporting to be the amount paid by Benswick in advance to Decca, when no such advance was made.
facts.F8: Expense account irregularities were also found, including reimbursement of expenditures unrelated to the Shanghai Centre, such as credit card slips for night clubs and sauna parlours in Hong Kong, duty free establishments at international airports, and a sports shop in Sydney, Australia.
facts.F9: The CFO, McNett, disappeared without explanation within the week of the investigation's beginning in March 2000, and was later found to have embezzled about US$4m from Seacliff between January 1996 and March 2000.
facts.F10: Howe, Benswick's owner and alter ego, opposed the blanket disclosure of Benswick's bank accounts, stating that it would be extremely prejudicial to Benswick as well as to its business associates.
facts.F11: The court considered Seacliff has done enough to establish that there is a good ground for thinking that money that found its way into Benswick's account with HSBC is its money as a result of a fraud committed against it.
facts.F12: The court also considered the remedial action would be a proprietary claim against funds in a Hong Kong bank account of a Hong Kong incorporated company.

reference_issues: Whether Seacliff has done enough to establish that there is a good ground for thinking that money that found its way into Benswick's account with HSBC is its money as a result of a fraud committed against it
Whether the application for pre-trial discovery of Benswick's bank accounts should be permitted

facts.F1: A building was erected on a plot of land in Shek O village on the island of Hong Kong without the approval or consent of the Building Authority, contravening section 14(1) of the Buildings Ordinance (Cap.123).
facts.F2: An application for approval had been submitted by an authorised person on behalf of the then owner of the lot on the 24th August 1989, but was disapproved by the Building Authority by a letter dated the 19th October 1989.
facts.F3: Building works were carried out, resulting in the erection of the three-storey building, notwithstanding a warning letter from the Building Authority dated the 7th November 1990.
facts.F4: On the 9th January 1991, the Building Authority gave notice to the then owners, inviting them to demolish the unauthorised building, and warning them that failure to do so would result in the making of a demolition order under section 24(1) of the Buildings Ordinance.
facts.F5: As a result, the Building Authority made a demolition order on the 30th January 1991, requiring the Respondent to demolish and remove the building within 21 days.
facts.F6: The Applicant wishes to now carry out the works itself and recover the cost thereof from the owner, and seeks a Closure Order under section 27 of Cap.123.
facts.F7: The Respondent appealed against the decision, but the appeal was dismissed, and the result was not announced until August 1992.
facts.F8: On the 8th October 1992, the Applicant issued a fresh notice of its intention to apply for a Closure Order on the 8th January 1993, but the Respondent again appealed against that decision, and the appeal was eventually dismissed in February 1993.
facts.F9: There are geographical differences that served as the basis for the distinctions in the statutory provisions relating to building control.
facts.F10: The Building Authority has a usual practice when seeking Closure Orders.
facts.F11: The application for a Closure Order and the supporting affirmations were filed in the District Court.

reference_issues: Whether section 27 of the Buildings Ordinance (Cap.123) infringes Articles 10, 14, and 22 of the Hong Kong Bill of Rights Ordinance (Cap.383).
Whether the Respondent has been denied a fair hearing by an impartial tribunal in the determination of its rights and obligations in a suit at law.
